what_it_does: Cloud providers are under pressure to track and charge for the carbon footprint — both the electricity consumed during operation and the carbon 'baked in' during manufacturing of the physical servers — attributable to each customer's workload. Fair-CO2 argues that existing attribution methods are unfair because they ignore two important realities: a server's manufacturing carbon should be spread proportionally to how much it is actually used (not just divided equally across time), and when multiple workloads share a machine, they slow each other down through interference, changing who is really responsible for what cost. The paper borrows a mathematical tool from economics — the Shapley value, originally developed to split windfalls fairly among players in a cooperative game — to define a theoretically fair allocation. Because computing the exact Shapley value becomes exponentially expensive as the number of workloads grows, Fair-CO2 uses fast approximations based on real-time utilization and colocation interference, validated against the exact solution through simulations.
